# Introduction

Data from triUmp. Question is: Is this drug effective in preventing aides on females specifically?

$H_0$ : No, drug is not effective at preventing aides in females.

$H_A$ : YES, drug is effective at preventing aides in females.

(A new  preventative aides drug (triUmpsal) is under test in clinical trials. Consider only the females, does this drug seem effective?  Hint - use dplyr to obtain that subpopulation with the filter command.)

# Results

## Descriptive Results

### Graphical Descriptive Results

<!--Graphical results here.  Make sure to show your code.  Provide appropriate labels for axes, giving units if possible, and provide a good title for the graph, too.  Use the graphical results to describe the patterns if any that exist in the data as focused toward the research question. Bottom line is to explain the features of the graph that are relevant to conforming or departing to what is expected by your null hypothesis !-->

```{r}
barchartGC(~treatment + infected,data=triUmp)
barchartGC(~treatment + infected,data=triUmp, type="percent")

```  

The graph suggests that a slightly higher number of people who take the placebo instead of the drug end up with aides.

Since we're only focused on the results of females we can also check this:

```{r}
barchartGC(~treatment + gender,data=triUmp)
barchartGC(~treatment + gender,data=triUmp, type="percent")

```  

As the previous graph suggests, a slightly higher number of people who take the placebo instead of the drug end up with aides. There is also a slightly higher amount of females in this study.

### Numerical Descriptive Results

```{r}
table1 <- xtabs(~treatment + infected, data=triUmp)
rowPerc(table1)
colPerc(table1)
```

From these results we can see that out of a 100 infected with aids, 40.87 had taken the drug and 59.13 had not. This suggests that individuals who had not taken the drug have a very slightly higher chance of being infected with aids.

Once again we can check females as well:

```{r}
table2 <- xtabs(~infected + gender, data=triUmp)
rowPerc(table2)
colPerc(table2)
```
```{r}
table2 <- xtabs(~treatment + gender, data=triUmp)
rowPerc(table2)
colPerc(table2)
```

out of 100 females, 48.39 have had the treatment and 51.61 have not. Additionally, out of both males and females with aids, females accounted for 34.49 out of 100%. So when we are accounting for this study's entire population of individuals infected with aids, we can divide by 34.49 to infer what percentage are female.
<!--Numerical results go here. Use the numerical results to describe the patterns if any that exist in the data as focused toward the research question!-->

## Inferential Results

```{r}
chisq.test(table1)
chisqtestGC(table1)
fisher.test(table1)
```

p value is 0.0000002761 which is less than 0.05. So we can reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the treatment is effective in some way at preventing aids in females.

# Discussion and Conclusion

Data from triUmp. Original question is: Is this drug effective in preventing aides on females specifically?

We reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is some relationship between the treatment drug and females infected with aides. More specifically, that females who have taken the drug have a slightly lower chance of being infected. The graphical summary and numerical results show that there are slightly fewer individuals out of a hundred who have taken the drug are infected, when compared to individuals that havent taken the drug and are infected. Because there are statistically more females than males in the study, we can infer that the results are still accurate when only focusing on females.
